utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, you can proceed to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Let's see whether there is something wrong with the monitor here. I don't have anything, and Judge Taya doesn't have anything -- yeah, it's come now. Sorry. Yes. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Anna Richterova and Julian Nicholls for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, madam, and to your team. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, on this 4th of July, Your Honours. And I appear here on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin along with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and our assistant Marela Jevtovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And good afternoon to you and your team. And our best regards on the occasion of your national day. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. So let's -- any preliminaries? No. Let's bring in the witness and continue from where he left yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to continue from where we left yesterday. In other words, you are practically going to start giving evidence today in substance. But before you do so, may I ask you to read out once more your solemn declaration to tell us the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Nicholls will be firing questions one after the other until exhaustion. Yes, Mr. Nicholls Examined by Mr. Nicholls: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, now, yesterday we didn't have very much time to start your testimony, and you had just told us about your background and that relationship -- the relations between the Serbian and non-Serbian population of Sanski Most had started breaking down towards the end of 1991. Do you remember whether civilian-owned property began to be blown up at night at any time during that period, late 1991, early 1992?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They started blowing up shops, business premises, and houses that belonged to Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who is they who you say started committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't go out at night. The perpetrators were never found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when these explosions -- to the best of your recollection, when did this blowing up of non-Serb property start? What's the first incident that you recall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a law office across the road from the court, Sarcevic Sabic -- this was towards the end of February in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember when the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade arrived when power was taken over in Sanski Most by force, between the 19th and 20th. But before that they were playing the key role. They had already been deployed at main points in the town. That's where they had been deployed. So it was not possible to get out of town without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was, if you know, Dusan Saovic? I hope I'm pronouncing that reasonably correctly.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Saovic was commander to the SOS unit in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that unit created for? Can you describe what role that unit had in Sanski Most in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they issued orders of the SDS party, which was led by Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment before you proceed to the next question -- next answer. Sir, you said the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived when power was taken over in Sanski Most by force between the 19th and the 20th. Could you tell us the month, please, because that is not reflected in the question or in the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my opinion, as far as I know, I know that that was in April, as far as I know. I don't know about what happened before because I didn't get around very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that the SOS -- the translation reads -- "issued orders of the SDS party."

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you clarify that. Did they issue orders to the SDS party or did they carry out orders issued by the SDS party to them?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They implemented the orders that the SDS issued to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Saovic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called him Njunja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that you didn't know who was blowing up this non-Serb property in Sanski Most, property owned by non-Serbs. And I don't know whether you were referring to you don't know the individuals or you don't know which groups were doing that. Could you clarify that for me.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he's been asked and it's been answered. He said he didn't know because he wasn't there. He wasn't out at night. I mean, I think he said what he knows about it. I object to any further questioning about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say to that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's that clear because he could be stating that he doesn't know the actual individuals who planted bombs at certain specific businesses or homes, but he might know which groups or organisations were carrying out these acts. And if he doesn't know, he can say he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if he wasn't out at night, like he said, and didn't know who was doing it, then how would he know what groups were doing it? I mean, the question was broad enough for him to answer it if he knows. It's been asked. It's been answered. I think we're done already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think as the question has been put, it has been answered already. If you want to rephrase it in some other way as to cover new ground, then you are allowed. But otherwise the objection [Realtime transcript read in error "organisation"] is sustained. Not the organisation -- the objection is sustained. It still remains the organisation. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to whether the SOS was carrying out bombings of non-Serb property? And please don't answer the question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's pretty leading, Your Honour. And it's the same question asked in a different way but in a leading way. And I object to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- him to rephrase the question in a different way. So as to cover -- he is begin specific now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's leading. He's now telling the witness who he thinks it was that was carrying out the bombings. It's pretty easy for the witness now to agree with him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but he said as to whether the SOS was carrying out bombings. In other words, he's not suggesting that SOS was and then asking the witness whether he has personal knowledge of it. It's -- it's -- no. The objection is not sustained now, and the witness is invited to answer the question. The question is, sir: Do you have any personal knowledge as to whether the SOS was carrying out bombings on non-Serb property? If you have personal knowledge as to whether the SOS was carrying out such bombings, you tell us yes and then you explain. If you don't, you tell us no and you don't need to explain anything further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't know. I didn't move around. In evening I didn't go out -- I didn't leave my house in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you -- when did you stop working at the courthouse in Sanski Most? In 1992 I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the 15th. A few days later on the municipal court in Sanski Most was taken over by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're speaking of the 15th of April, 1992, when you say the 15th?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what you mean by -- when you say the courthouse was taken over. What do you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, in the morning, when we turned up at our jobs, three or four vehicles arrived. They were terrain vehicles, civilian and military ones. They blocked the court -- they surrounded the court, and that's the fist time that I met Mr. Vrkes. That's how he introduced himself. He was with his bodyguard who was wearing a military uniform and had an automatic rifle. They entered the building, and they said that we should all gather in a courtroom, room number 8, and with them was Milan Stolic, who was a retired policeman whom they had sent, and they removed someone who was at the door called Lisic Sefik, so Lisic Sefik had to leave his post and Mr. Stolic took over his job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Vrkes? How did he introduce himself? What authority did he tell you he had to hold this meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he entered the courtroom, we all sat down. There were benches. He then introduced himself and he said that his name was Vlado Vrkes and that he was there on behalf of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any -- you and the other court personnel, did you have any advance notice of this visit by Mr. Vrkes with his armed guards? Did you know this was going to happen when you went to work that day?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We turned up at work in the morning. We weren't expecting something like that to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any -- were there any demands made upon you and the other court personnel? Were there any requests of acts that you would have to comply with in order to keep your jobs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead here. You can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required to take any kind of oath that day by Mr. Vrkes? Was that demanded of you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were asked to sign a pledge of loyalty in order to be able to continue working in the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't need the exact wording, but if you can describe a little bit what that pledge stated and what entity you would be pledging loyalty to if you signed that oath or pledge.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that document because I didn't sign any such pledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you refuse to sign that pledge?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had signed that pledge, then I would have been a second class citizen, a second class man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Could you explain why that would make you a second class person to sign that oath, or you felt that way.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have had to carry out their orders. I would have been a servant in a certain sense. And the same would have happened if -- even if I hadn't signed it, because the same thing happened. We lost our jobs a few days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A servant to whom?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been -- Mr. Vrkes said that today the court would be under Bosnian Krajina, under the authority of Bosnian Krajina, and that we had to respect their laws and their rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many employees were -- refused to sign that oath and subsequently lost their jobs in the next couple of days?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about ten of us, ten of us Muslims, and there was a Croatian lady. I don't know about her, because she was married to a Croat -- to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb employees of the court who were forced to leave their jobs?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same occasion are you saying that 40 Serb employees were forced to leave their jobs because they refused to sign a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any of them signing a pledge of loyalty, and they continued to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe that about a week after this -- after you lost your job you moved out of your house in Sanski Most. Can you tell us why that was?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left my house. I lived in the Alagica Polje neighbourhood with my parents, who lived in Mahala and with my brother and sister-in-law for the same reason, because on the 23rd of May in the evening my house was blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at home when your house was blown up? How did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Over the weekend I usually went to my wife's mother, so I was in -- with her in the village of Caplje over that weekend. And that morning my brother phoned me. He wasn't able to tell me, but he said that there was a leak in my house. I didn't understand how there could have been a leak, since I had checked everything and I had cut -- I had shut the water off, and then I went to Caplje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of neighbourhood was your house in, the one that was blown up, the Alagica Polje neighbourhood? What was the predominant ethnicity in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of the population was Serbian. I was the only Muslim in the street with my wife and son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, being the only non-Serb in that street, were you speaking now about just before the house was blown up -- did you feel comfortable living there, in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that situation had already started in April. I didn't really feel safe, so my wife and child went to Croatia. I hoped that this would be over very soon; however, what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you report to anybody this criminal act, somebody blowing up part of your house?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, I took my car, I went to Mahala, I fetched my brother and father, and then I saw what happened when I arrived there. My father and brother remained in the house. I went to the police to report the explosion, to report the fact that my house had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the police do in response to your report?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they would go to the site. I returned home. And later on two inspectors arrived to carry out an investigation -- on on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they carry that investigation out? Did you get a sense that this crime that you were a victim of was being taken seriously or was not being taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take that very seriously. I -- in previous occasions when cafes had been blown up, these cases were never solved, so similarly my case wasn't solved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said cafes. These cafes and homes were being blown up. Just to be completely clear, were any of these to your knowledge owned by Serbs, or were they all owned by people of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to people of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After -- well, was the damage to your home so severe that you couldn't continue to live in it even if -- even if you had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kitchen and another room remained intact, however that was a warning issued to me. They wanted to tell me that I shouldn't live there any more, so it wasn't a good idea to continue living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who's they? You said they wanted to issue you a warning.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the perpetrators were, because I wasn't at home so I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this explosion at your home, are you aware of whether these types of incidents continued to occur in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 26th and 27th, when the attack in Mahala took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you tell me about that now. Where did you go around the 26th, since you could no longer live in your home, you didn't feel safe there.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th in the morning I went to Mahala, to my parents' place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened that day when you arrived in Mahala? What do you remember happening?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going into town on a bike, and in front of the department store there was an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we got that all. Let me ask you the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you talk quite a lot about what happened to you and your parents in Mahala that day and how you were in the basement of the house and there was some shelling. Can you describe that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, my mother, and father went to my brother's, who was renting a place, and he had a basement. And we were there about 7.00 or 8.00, and the shelling started between 8.00 and 9.00. He was the only one who had a basement there, so that the neighbours also came to that basement to seek shelter, women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in that basement with you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 25 to 30 women, children, and old men, my whole family, my father, my brother, my sister-in-law, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any warning that this shelling of Mahala was about to start? Was there any kind of warning to you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no prior warning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know, do you know who -- who or which armed forces were shelling Mahala that day?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 6th Krajina Brigade that was shelling from the surrounding hills where they were positioned around Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were out in Mahala and when you arrived there, did you see any armed groups of non-Serbs? Did you see any rebel paramilitary formations on the streets?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Everything was deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was the threat to the 6th Krajina Brigade or to the Serb people from Mahala the day that shelling was happening?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no threat. There was no resistance. Just the people who were powerless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that basement and also how long did the shelling continue?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling went on from 9.00 in the evening until the next day at 9.00 or 9.30 in the morning, the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after the shelling stopped? What did you and those other people in the basement do?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't all go out. The owner's father went into the house. He switched on the radio and listened, and there were announcements broadcast every five minutes calling on the population to come out and to gather at the exercise ground where people were training for drivers, for their driving licence test, and this was a large area with a fence round it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, if you remember, were there any other demands made over the radio, specifically referring to the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't, because we were in the basement, so that we were isolated and we didn't dare go out until it stopped. And he went out to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then tell me about how you left the house and where you went after -- after you'd heard about these announcements on the radio.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late in the afternoon everything was deserted when we left that basement, and we formed a column and we went from upper Mahala towards lower Mahala. By then Mahala had been completely abandoned. The people had already left. We didn't know that. We were left alone in that basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mahala look like after you came out and started walking through it? Could you see any results from the shelling? Did you see any damage? Can you describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the second half of Mahala, where we were stopped, and from there towards town, we saw the damage and some houses burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just briefly describe to the Chamber the extent of that damage to the town, how many houses you saw damaged or burning. If you don't remember, that's -- that's okay.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this soldier led us down there towards town, where he left us for the night, we came across a couple of houses that were burning, and we saw a soldier throw a cocktail grenade into one house and it burst up in flames suddenly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then tell us what happened. You said you were walking through town and you stopped and you spent the night. Just -- if you can just continue. What happened to this group of people that you were walking through Sanski Most with? Can you tell me where you spent the night -- the next night after you came out of the basement and walked through town.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent the night in a house, in a basement owned by a Sarcevic. This was just before night-time. There were another ten people there, a total of 40 of us in that basement which was close to the river and it was cold and damp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at some point were you given permission to leave that area?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We stayed there all night until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the owner of that building, Sarcevic, called up the Crisis Staff to see what he should do with so many people, because he couldn't accommodate them any longer. But he didn't get any answer. And outside was a guard who went off. There was no one. And we spontaneously headed towards a settlement. I had an aunt up there, my father, my mother, and myself. Other people went in a different direction, I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was at a place in Sanski Most called Narodni front?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a housing district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move on now to the very end of May. I believe you heard another radio announcement telling you that you and your family had to report somewhere. If that's right, can you tell me about that radio announcement and what you did.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day the population who were not residents of the Narodni front were called upon, because there were quite a number of families from Mahala who had relatives there, and we all went to the football pitch of the Narodni front elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these families from Mahala who were at Narodni front, they were there because -- why were they there at that point? Why hadn't they gone back to Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not allowed to go to Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the elementary school when you arrived with your parents?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the football pitch in front of the elementary school and in front of the sports hall. Then us men were separated into the sports hall and the women and children were taken back. I don't know. My mother and father were also told to go back because they were elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were 61 and 62 years old; is that right? Something like that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the men being held with you at the sports hall who were not released, who were not told to go back, what -- what ethnicity were these men who were held at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Muslims, mostly from Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Citizens or members of --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, citizens of Muslim ethnicity. Mostly people who used to live in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe from your statement you spent seven days at the sports hall. Can you tell me if that's correct and then what happened after that seven days when you were released.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in this small hall, we spent the whole day there. And towards dusk they escorted us to the sports hall. And when we entered, there were a couple of thousand men already there from Mahala. It was only there that I learnt two days later that my two brothers were alive, an older and a younger brother. I found them there in the hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you held in that hall? And if you can just very briefly describe what the conditions were like while you were held there, what you slept on and what you had to eat and drink.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for seven days. We slept on the parquet floor. We were given water, but frequently there was none. The conditions were impossible. We couldn't bathe, and very often the water supply -- there was no water in the taps. The food would come occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why -- why you were being held there and why you couldn't leave, given any explanation?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any contact with anyone. We were detained there. So I had no contact with anyone outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was detaining you and the other men at that -- at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards who were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us how you came to be released from that detention facility.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when I was released there was a large convoy, 10 to 12 buses. Inside were women and children, and then they filled up the buses with men from the sports hall. And someone said, "As my settlement was mostly Serbian and it was not a war zone, I was told I could go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go back to your house, the one that had been -- the one you told us about that had been damaged by an explosion?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go back. I didn't dare. But I went to my neighbour's in another street where there were more Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point soon after that, were you taken back into custody? Were you arrested again? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 5th of June, 1992 in the morning they were looking for me at a neighbour's. They asked him where this other house was. And four military policemen came and asked me whether my name was Bekir Delic. They said -- I said yes, and they said, "You must come with me for an information interview at the police station."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say -- how do you know these were military policemen who came to get you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had military uniforms and white belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? What happened during -- tell us where they brought you and what happened to you after they picked you up.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to the police station. We parked the car. We entered the corridor. And they told me to lean against the wall, to turn around, and to wait until the inspector called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long -- and then at some point did the inspector come to interview you and to interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Another inspector came, Dusko Zoric, who took me to his office to interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this man Dusko Zoric from -- is this the first time you had met him, or did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew him from before, because we lived in the same street when we both got married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me about what happened next. What happened during that interrogation with this person that you knew?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This didn't last long, his interrogation, because soon after that Brane Sobot, also an inspector, came, who had sent the policemen to fetch me to interview me. Dusko Zoric started yelling at me as if he'd never seen me before, and he was holding a weapon. I don't know much about weapons, so I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did this go on, this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. And then they took me to the next-door office, that is, inspector Brane Sobot took me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you're talking about this building you're in now, the police station, that is also known as the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You need to answer for the microphone, because we're recording this.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was the answer yes or no that this was the MUP that you were being held in at this point?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before it was called the SUP. Now it is called the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you weren't beaten during these interrogations, but you were shouted at and you were questioned about weapons and anything you knew about weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I didn't know anything about that. I was an ordinary citizen who had spent the three years prior to the war building my house, so I didn't have any time for anything else except to devote my time to the building of my house and to my family that I had just formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, before this arrest, did you in fact own any weapons, any firearms?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this interrogation, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a couple of hours, the inspector left, and he said I should go to the prison and that he would continue later. And in the corridor, there was a policeman, Drago Dosenovic, known as Maco, and Ivica Pranic was also waiting in the corridor, a Croat, and he took both of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went downstairs. The offices were upstairs. We followed him, and he -- he opened the door and we entered a police car called a Golf, a Golf police car, and we headed towards town. It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he take you in this police car?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I know the town well, we passed by the court, and then we turned towards the Hasan Kikic elementary school. We entered the yard and stopped behind the gym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened there? I don't think you were there for very long. Can you tell us what happened there and where you were brought to next, where you were finally imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dosenovic handed us over to the guards. There were three of them there wearing reserve police uniforms. He turned back, and when we entered they closed the door. They told us to take off our laces. They asked whether we had any money or anything. This was a small hall with the sports equipment inside. Then they opened the door of the large hall. We entered, and it was full of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you spend at this place before you were taken to the Betonirka garage?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just spent the night there. In the morning, together with the others, after breakfast a policeman came, who read out a list of seven or eight names. He told us to go into a smaller room and to sit down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were in there for just a short time and you were told to write out some statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened next? If you can tell us, just briefly after you -- after that incident.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a formality for us to write down something. We didn't write anything. About five times -- five minutes later Dusan Saovic, known as Njunja, passed through the corridor. I knew him. And they entered and shut the door. We just heard trucks outside, and a policeman came, who told us to get in. There was no one there. The hall was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened to all those other people who had been in the hall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first transport of people from that hall to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, where do you go next from here? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A young policeman came and said that we should go out three by three and get into a car, and he drove us to the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the Betonirka," that's what you're referring to as the prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were three garages there, concrete garages with iron doors. They were garages used for cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have the witness take a look at P824.1. And I suppose we should put this on the ELMO so that everybody can see it. Could you try to -- I don't know if it's possible to get the whole photo on. It doesn't appear to be on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, if you could look at this photo -- and if it's easier, you can look at the paper photo to your right -- at P824.1. Can you look at that for a second and tell me if you recognise the garages in that photo.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the garages, 1, 2, and 3, of Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this photograph was not taken in 1992. Is this a fair and reasonably accurate photograph of what the garages looked like back when you were there in 1992 in June?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as they are on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have the witness shown P824.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at that. Is that a reasonably fair and accurate picture of the interior, of what the garages looked like from the inside?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness two more photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They're new ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. These are new ones which have not yet -- this will be P845.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if you could look at that photo for a minute and tell me whether that is a fair and accurate representation of the interior of the Betonirka garages as you remember it from June 1992.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here is the last one, which will be P846.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if you could take a look at that. Tell me whether that looks like the interior of the garages looking out in 1992 and if those doors look similar to the doors there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These holes weren't in the doors, and this hole above wasn't there either, but this window was there. But on the outside there were two concrete blocks. There was very little air because they blocked the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through that now. Thank you. When you arrived at Betonirka, were you told why you were being placed in one of these garages? Or tell me what happened right when you first arrived at Betonirka garage.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were taken there in three shifts. We were driven there to the Betonirka. And the guard who was there opened the garage. We came three by three. There were seven or eight of us. We were in groups. We entered the garage. There was nothing inside. There was just that concrete, concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you told how long you were going to be held there? Did you have any idea how long you were going to spend in that concrete garage?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one told me anything. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you charged with any offence? Were you told you had -- were suspected of committing any crime or anything like that before you were locked up in there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people that first night were locked up with you in that first garage?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about seven or eight of us. We had been separated from that big group and put into that first garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the people who were held with you? I'm speaking now right at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember individual names. Osman Talic was there, the police commander Enver Burnic, Nihad Kljucanin, Karabeg Rasim, Pranic Ivica, Neno Alagic, and myself. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend in total in that garage? How many days?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent 31 days there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to start telling us what conditions were like and what the daily routine, for lack of a better phrase, was like for you in Betonirka garages. We've seen what the interior of the cell looked like and you've said it was similar back then, except those holes were not in the doors. You started telling us about the windows. How many windows were there in your cell and were you able to open those windows?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a window which we couldn't open, and I said when we got there they had placed those concrete blocks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we saw that there was a door to that cell -- to the garage - excuse me - were you allowed to -- was that door normally kept open or closed? And if it was closed, was it locked or unlocked?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were inside, and if we didn't go to have breakfast or lunch, it was usually closed. But when we went to have breakfast or when we went to have lunch, obviously it would be open for us to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the greatest number of men that you can remember being held in that cell with? Because I think that people would come and go. You correct me if I'm wrong -- that some people would be released, others would come in. Can you tell me what the greatest number of people who were forced to stay in that cell.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 25 people. They started opening up, and they would then put people in the second and third garage when others arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean when one garage would fill up, then they would start filling up the second and then the third?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I want to say. When one garage would be filled up, then they would use the second and then the third. There were three garages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, obviously we can tell from those photos that there were no showers or toilet facilities or running water in the garages. Can you tell us what facilities you were provided with for bathing and for going to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any water for bathing. All we had was some sort of field toilet. If they allowed us to we would use this field toilet. That was a little further away. It was in the grounds of Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "if they allowed us to." Can you explain that. Were you not -- when were you allowed to and when were you not allowed to use the field toilet?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually when we had breakfast or lunch we asked if we could use the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would you do if you were not given permission? What would you have to do?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion we were given bad food which had been left outside in the heat, so people had stomach cramps and pains. And I apologise. I have to say this. They had -- people had to relieve themselves into nylon bags because they wouldn't open the doors and let us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber some more about what food you were provided with during those 31 days or so that you were held there.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning we usually had tea and a slice of bread for breakfast. Food would be brought in from the kitchen for lunch, which was in the MUP building. The kitchen was in the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this good food? Did you have enough to eat? Did you feel that you were being adequately provided for?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sometimes we weren't even able to eat that food because the guards asked us -- demanded that we eat it in five minutes' time. And this food was very hot, so you could only take a slice of bread and return to the garage. Otherwise we would have burned ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about water? Were you given enough water and --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have enough water, but we were given water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the temperature like in that garage in the summer of 1992 when you were held there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The temperatures were very high. You could imagine. We were surrounded by concrete. The windows were blocked. The door was a metal door. So on one day when Martic, the commander of the shift, was there -- he didn't let us have lunch or breakfast. We were shut in all day long, and it was impossible to endure this. People just fainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many hours a day would you typically spend in that garage with all those other men? You said you had five minutes to run out and get food, so I'm wondering how long you would normally have to spend in the garage.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said -- I've just mentioned one occasion. It depended on the shift that was there. Sometimes we would spend half an hour outside. That was the maximum. But as I have said -- I've told you about this case. There was a case in the evening too. We were ordered that we -- to stand up from 7.00 in the evening up until 7.00 in the morning, and we weren't allowed to sleep. And Martic, the shift commander, ordered Kravic Milan the guard to control us every ten minutes -- to check to see if someone had fallen asleep. If someone had sat down, that person knew what he could expect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could that person expect, somebody who hadn't obeyed that order and had fallen asleep?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that person would be taken away to a room. There was another office -- another hut which was used as an office, since it was a construction firm. And that person would then be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were people taken out of your garage, the one you were held at, and beaten?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average for several hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question though is: How often would somebody be taken out and beaten? Not how long they would be beaten for, but how many times a day or how often in a week would somebody be taken out and be beaten by the guards?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very seldom that someone would not be beaten. Usually when people were arrested or captured they had to go through this torture when entering the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what these people would look like when they came back from being beaten, what -- what a prisoner -- what you would -- what they would look like, what you would see when somebody came back from being beaten.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see that they had difficulty in enduring those blows and the pain. You could see that they had cramps. You couldn't touch anyone anywhere. If you touched anyone, the -- you'd be told, "Don't touch me. That hurts me -- it hurts me here. It hurts me everywhere."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally beaten while you were held there for that period?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only on one occasion by Martic. I was hit by Martic. I was slapped by Martic on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Martic -- this Martic you're speaking of, do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. He was the shift commander. He'd been born in Kljevci. He was a lot younger than I was, so I can't remember that. He grew up in Kljevci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ran the Betonirka prison? Do you know who was in charge of running it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Vujanic ran it and Krunic Milorad was the deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these policemen, civilians? Can you describe which authority was in charge of this prison?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Vujanic was a lawyer by profession. So he was the chief of the department where passports and identity cards were issued, whereas Milorad Krunic was a retired policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were any types of people, did it seem to you, specially selected for beatings or for mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't make any difference. If it was an ordinary man or a Muslim, they didn't pay attention to -- to differences. They didn't distinguish between anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let mow just ask you about something in your statement. You talk about a man named Enver Burnic. Can you describe how he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, on the 28th of June, that's when they had a religious day. Martic came. He was drunk. He came in the afternoon with two young men, 16 and 17 years of age. They were wearing police uniforms. They called him and asked him to come out, and the guards took him to that room, to those offices, where people would be tortured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? Did you see him after he came back, Mr. Burnic?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He begged them to stop beating him. He said that he would rather they killed him. However, Martic said, "A bullet is too costly for you. You're going to die. That's for sure. But your death will be a slow one."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Burnic's job or position before he'd been arrested and locked up with you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a police commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were any of these people who were locked up in that cell with you -- to your knowledge were any of these people involved in any form of armed resistance or rebellion?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of people were they who were being held in there with you, held in the Betonirka garages while you were there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were ordinary citizens from Sanski Most, and they were of Muslim ethnicity. And there were Croats too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've talked about these beatings that occurred on a -- I think it's -- what I'm getting from what you say, a daily basis. Was any medical care provided for the victims?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The people who came, they would return to the garage. We'd give them water if we had any. We would put wet cloths on them. That's the only thing we could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you weren't physically beaten. You've told us that. But what happened to you physically as a result of being kept in this small room with that many men in that heat for 31 days? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lost some weight, and I felt ill later on, since there was a concrete floor and it was cold. I had problems and I had haemorrhoids, so I had terrible pains for four or five days. And that was due to the bad nutrition and to the conditions we were in and to everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that time you were there were you able to change your clothes at all, were you able to wash your clothes, or did you -- how long did you have to keep wearing the same set of clothes that you wore when you were arrested and when you were brought in?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only on one occasion, on the 11 of June. My elder brother brought me a change of clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm almost done talking about this topic, but if you know who was actually doing the beatings? You say that men were brought out of the cells and taken and were beaten and then were brought back and you could see that they'd been severely beaten. But who -- who was beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the worst shift was when Commander Milan Cetkovic, known as Dzo Banana was there, and the guard Veselinovic whose first name I don't know. Martic when he was the guard commander and Milan Kravic, another guard, Milenko Mrkanovic, Savo Mrkanovic, that was another shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Cetkovic, the person you say with the nickname Banana, why was his shift -- why do you call that the worst shift?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because torture would take place during their shifts, and that happened during his shift when the food was left outside in the -- in the sun. I don't know how you would interpret this, but he said that after we had been poisoned, he said, "It would be better for my pigs to eat this food than you balijas, you Muslims." We had food poisons, we who were in the first garage, and we banged on the door and begged them to open the door but they wouldn't let us go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is fairly obvious too, but with that many men in one of these garages to just hold a single vehicle, was there enough room at night for everybody to sleep? Were you able to sleep at night?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was impossible to sleep because you'd -- you were expecting to be called out at any time, because they took people away to beat them. So it was very rarely that one was able to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know we'll probably be breaking in about seven minutes. If -- I'm going to move on to a new topic. I don't know if you prefer to break early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That suits us fine. We will break now, resuming at five to 4.00, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question I should have asked you before we broke, about the men that you were held with in the Betonirka garages. What was the age range of your fellow prisoners, to the best of your memory? What was the youngest -- the age of the youngest person there and the age of the oldest person there based on your personal knowledge of the 31 days that you were held in the garage?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The youngest was about 20, and the oldest was about 65.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me try to refresh your recollection. Do you remember making a statement and giving it to the Office of the Prosecutor investigator?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll move on. I want to start talking now about how you came to leave Betonirka garage and transferred -- were transferred to Manjaca camp. And we'll go through this step by step. First of all, can you tell me what the date was. What's the last -- what day was the last morning you remember being at the Betonirka garages?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that morning did you know you were going to be leaving Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know. It was only after breakfast when the call-out started. Seven or eight men were separated, and they were taken to the SUP, and we stayed on in the garages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, just for clarity, the SUP is also what is now known as the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that building was just behind the Betonirka garages, a short ways behind it, across a field.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just behind the Betonirka construction company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What were you told after breakfast about how you were going to be leaving the camp -- the garages?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know anything. But I asked a guard called Savo, "Tell us what's happening." And he said, "You're going to Manjaca." And I asked, "Am I going too?" And he said, "You're first on the list."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day was it when you actually left the garage, when you were told, "Okay. Out"?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left when we all got onto the truck and it was closed, it was about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- what kind of -- what was the temperature at noon that day?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the month of July, the summer, and it was very hot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men from your garage were taken out to be put on this truck?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all three garages people were called out, and you lined up and got onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've talked a lot about beatings at the Betonirka garages. Was anybody beaten that morning or that day before leaving?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rufad Zukic was called out by a guard called Veselinovic, and he took him to this office where he was beaten up and he came back crawling, and we had to draw him -- drag him into the garage. Also a Croat who was beaten by soldiers, and they brought the handle of -- broke the handle of a broom over him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "crawling," do you mean that literally? Crawling on his hands and knees? Or do you --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On all fours, yes. On his knees and hands. He had been beaten so badly that he couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally threatened in any way or beaten?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This guard Veselinovic came inside and started from the door. I was standing in the corner and he was holding a knife. He came up to me, pointed the knife at my neck, and asked me, "How are you doing, Delic?" What could I answer but saying yes. And then he said, "Take off everything you have on your hands because it will be taken anyway at Manjaca."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the truck pulls up in front of the garages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the truck to the Chamber, as best as you can remember it.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. We were called out in order according to the list, and we all had to run out. We had to run between two lines and climb onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Run between two lines of what? What do you mean by "run between two lines"?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two lines of guards, policemen, just in case anyone were to try to go outside these two lines so as to make sure that we got onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to anybody while they were running between those two lines of people to get onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This went on very quickly. I was among the first to get onto the truck, so I climbed right to the front of the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my earlier question, which I'm not sure you understood, was to describe the truck. Can you just tell Their Honours whether this was a civilian truck if you know or a military truck and about how large the compartment was where the prisoners had -- were loaded into, how high it was, how wide it was, and how long it was.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a civilian truck, not very big. I don't know the exact size, but it was too small for the number of men who got on. There was an orange rubbery tarpaulin, but I don't know exactly how long and how wide it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't expect you to remember the exact dimensions. That's okay. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You said it was too small for the amount of men. Do you remember how many men got on the truck?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 60 or so. About 60. Maybe one or two more. And it was too small, so we sat in each other's lap. We couldn't really move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was a rubber -- rubber sort of orange tarpaulin. Can you describe how that was attached to the truck, how tightly and how much space was left between the tarpaulin and the truck.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was tightened, as it is normal to do for transport. And if anyone were to try to do anything, we would get beaten with a truncheon. There were policemen walking round the truck all the time, so that we couldn't try to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were one of the first people onto the truck. What -- where did you -- what position did you take? Where were you sitting or standing?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in the corner at the front, from the -- when you are looking from the cabin backwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that it wasn't big enough for all these men, these 60 or so men, and that you were kind of sitting on each other. And in your statement, you said you were like sardines. When you were at the front behind the cab, can you -- was it so tight that you were being pushed into it, or did you have room to move around at all? I want you to try to describe how packed it was in that truck, if you can.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any space. We were so packed that we couldn't move around. We would trample on each other. That was the only way to move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any rips, holes, or openings in this tarpaulin or any way that you could open it yourself from the inside if you wanted to look out or get some air?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was the first right up there, while we were parked I tried to look through a small hole through which the rope is threaded to tighten the tarpaulin to see where we were, and when I peeped out -- it's a small hole -- I was hit with a truncheon, so that after that I didn't even try, because he said if anyone tried, he would kill us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be clear, other than that small hole or eyelet which you tried to look out which you said was for tying the tarpaulin down with the ropes, were there any other holes, or was that the only type of hole in the tarpaulin is what I'm trying to ask you.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any. Everything was very tight. If we would try to push with our own hands, again, we would get blows and threats that they would kill us if we tried to do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you got on the truck about noon. And it was closed up, I take it. You were locked in there. You said you couldn't get out. Where did the truck go and what time did it leave? Did it leave right at noon, or were you on the truck awhile before it left?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to the sports hall where another 500 or 600 men who had been detained there from Mahala joined us. And we stood there for about three or four hours. And the heat was the worst there. You can imagine. In the sunshine when you're standing there, there's no shade. There's nothing to protect you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "standing there," you mean that the truck was parked outside the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were parked there, and we were waiting for the rest of the men to get on. But this took a long time, so that during those first few hours already people started to lose consciousness. They were crying out for help, but there was no help coming. There was a young man of 17, and he was the first to start fainting. We tried to revive him by slapping him, but he had turned blue already. And a couple of kilometres later on our way to Manjaca he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first got on the truck at Betonirka with all these people, were you given any food and water for the journey ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When people were called out, only just one man managed to get a bit of water. But even that small amount of water didn't help him survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were parked at the sports hall -- I think it's clear, but just to be certain -- for those hours, was anybody allowed off of the truck? Was anybody provided with any water at that point?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We couldn't get off. I said before, if we were to try to do anything, to move the tarpaulin with our hand, we would be beaten and threatened, that if we didn't stop we would get killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to move the tarpaulin at all yourself and were you beaten at all? I'm speaking of you personally.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the first occasion that I told you about, when I peeped through that hole, and that is when I got a blow. After that I didn't try again, and I couldn't anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then while you were parked at the sports hall, that's when people began to faint or pass out from the heat.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People already started to pass out, and they started tearing off their clothes. It was intolerable. This was a life-and-death struggle, which many failed to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the first person to die was this 17-year-old man -- young man. Do you remember his last name or first name?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hukanovic Sevdaga from Vrhpolje. He was detained in the SUP, and that day he was brought from the cell in the SUP to be transported to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when that young man died, that was while the truck was already moving again. Correct me if I'm wrong. That was after you'd left the parking area at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had already set off on the journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please continue. Tell me what happened on that next part of the journey after leaving the sports hall as you went towards Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was dreadful. People were struggling to remain alive. They were trying to catch some air in one way or another, and there was no chance. It just depended on the strength of the organism, because people had already been mistreated and there was no water and people started to drink their own urine, so it was really dreadful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain on that truck from leaving the sports hall until it arrived at Manjaca? How long was that journey -- that part of the journey?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About eight to nine hours. It was a long journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time -- I know it's difficult for you to tell, but what time do you think it was approximately when you arrived at Manjaca, when the truck finally stopped there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 9.00. The sun had set when we got there. When the truck was parked and when they lifted the tarpaulin and told us to get off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent about -- and all the other men spent about nine hours on that truck with the tarpaulin tied down from leaving Betonirka till the arrival, is that right, arrival at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said the sun was setting or had set when you arrived. When you got to Manjaca, what happened? What did you see? Were you allowed off the truck right away, or did it park there and did you stay on it for some time? Describe what happened at the end of this journey.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived there and when the truck stopped, the other trucks with trailers were parked behind us with the men from the sports hall. Then they opened the tarpaulin and then they said that we should get off. However, it was only then that we saw what had happened with the men who were with me on the truck. We were told to get off, whereas I and two other men were told to take out the bodies of 17 or 18 men who had suffocated or had a heat stroke or whatever - I don't know myself - and then these others who were alive were lined up outside and stood waiting. So we carried them all out and lined them up where we were told to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said in your statement -- you characterise the way these men died as slow and agonising, that they would pant for air, hallucinate, finally faint, and that you would try to slap them back into consciousness to keep them aware or alive and it didn't work. Is that -- do you stand by that statement? Is that accurate, or do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever you have said is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once they lifted that tarpaulin - and I take it that's when you realised how many people had died - were there any people amongst -- on your truck who had not died but who were ill or in very bad shape?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those men who were in poor shape, we carried them out too and lined them up together with those who had already died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately -- I don't expect you to remember - maybe you do - how many men were there who needed -- who were still alive at this point but who needed to be carried off the truck because they couldn't move themselves?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 35, counting us as well who were carrying out the dead, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said when you got there, and they pulled back the tarpaulin. Who was it who started giving orders when you arrived? Who said you guys get off the truck, you carry the dead, you help those people who are sick, who was giving orders at that point?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the policemen who were in the transport and the leader of the convoy in a car accompanying the convoy was Dosenovic Drago, also known as Maca, and also there was the warden of the camp nicknamed Spaga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who -- who was the warden of the camp? What was his position? You've said his name and that he was a warden, but was he a policeman, a soldier, a civilian authority? Do you know who was in charge of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say or do when he -- when he saw that this transport had arrived and that there were 17 or 18 men who had died on the way? What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the men who were on their feet and who were all right should enter the camp and those who were dead and who were lying down should be taken back to Sanski Most and that the people from Sanski Most should be held responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
