utterances.text: And is that what happened? Were the -- what happened then to the people who --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before that he called the three of us, among those who were -- who had survived, and the policeman Mrsic who was nearby, he spoke to Enver Burnic, and a Croat, Vicko Mauzner, and he told them to get off and help these men. And the warden Spaga asked whether there was a doctor around to help these people, so that in this transport behind us there was some 500 or 600 other men from the sports hall -- Biscevic answered, a twin, the son of Faik, who was a dentist by profession, and he stayed there. And it was already dark and we were ordered to go inside into the camp. We entered, 50 in a line at a time. So these stayed behind me, so I don't know what happened to them, those who were dead and the few that were still alive. Those men are registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just make sure this is clear. Mr. Burnic, Mr. Mauzner, and Mr. Mauzner were ordered to load the bodies of the dead back on the truck and help those who were still alive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These bodies were already on the ground, and they told them, "We don't know. We entered the camp, and those who were lying down remained there. And the transport escort -- I know nothing else. They are listed as missing. We then entered the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this dentist -- you said somebody named Biscevic who was on a different truck answered the call as somebody who was willing to try to help.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and he separated from the group and went to where these people were lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation -- the transcript on page 43, line 22 has Mr. Mauzner and Mr. Mauzner twice. I think for clarify it was only -- I said it once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what -- that's what we heard. And I think that's what you said, because I -- I perfectly remember you saying Mr. Mauzner twice, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know what happened to these three men who stayed outside to help while you went into the camp?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We tried to find out, when after a long period of time we were able to establish contact, because there was the first camp and the second camp in Manjaca, but no one knew anything because it was already night -- no one knew what had happened to those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks -- you've talked about your -- the small truck that you were on. How many other trucks when you got off at Manjaca -- could you tell how many trucks there were in total in that on -- convoy to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About four or five trailers, big ones. I think about a hundred people could get in them. There were about 500 or 600 of us who were transported to Manjaca on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P698, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy, Mr. Nicholls, to put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at that. It's a 1st Krajina Corps command report from the 8th of July, 1992, and it's got at the top "Strictly confidential. Number 44/1-223." Is that the same document that you have before you in your language?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a combat report to the main staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item 4, situation on the ground, where it says: "Gradual mopping up of the Kotor Varos area. During the afternoon of 7 July, 1992, 600 prisoners of war were brought from Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. The interpreter who is translating into English for us, please speak into the microphone. Because I know that you are translating, but we can't hear a single word of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, let me stop you, sir, and ask a question. We can go on that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, yes. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in you look at item 4, which I think is what you had begun to look on yourself, that reads: "Gradual mopping up of the Kotor Varos area continues. During the afternoon of 7 July 1992, 600 prisoners of war were brought from Sanski Most." And then if we skip to section 5, it states that "There have been no unusual incidents." Is that what your -- is that what you read on your B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that figure of 600 prisoners would -- on the 7th of July would correspond to what you've told us about the amount of men you believe were transferred to Manjaca that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the convoy that I mentioned in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you some questions now about what it was like for you while you were in Manjaca camp. But first of all, can you tell me how long you were imprisoned at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there from the 7th of July, 1992 up until the 14th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, the same questions I asked you about when you arrived at Betonirka. Were you told how long you would be kept there? Were you told why you were there? Were you charged with any crime or given an explanation of why you were not -- why you were being held a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't explain anything to us, and we didn't have any contact with them. We were just imprisoned. We were just placed in those stables. That's what they called them. There were two camps with three big stables and up to 600 people on average could be placed in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you -- if you know, who was guarding the inside of the camp? Who were the guards on the inside of the camp, as opposed to the outside?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the camp there were guards, and then at the gate to the camp. When we arrived, there were reserve policemen from Kljuc there. Later policemen from Sanski Most came who were also guards, and they guarded us. And finally, there were military policemen, guards who stood guard over us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think after the conditions you've described that you were held in at Betonirka, over all conditions at Manjaca were an improvement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't better because we were put in the stables and we had to lie down on the ground. There was nothing there. The conditions were nonexistent. It's not possible for me to say that the conditions were any better than those at Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Manjaca, were you personally beaten?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But the following day, on the 8th, they started calling 20 people out to go for questioning, and they would return from this questioning after having been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, what types of people were with you in your stable in Manjaca? If you can just briefly describe whether these were civilians or soldiers or rebels or people involved in any kind of armed resistance. If you know, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These people were ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you personally see anybody murdered in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But Mr. Sabanovic came -- Mr. Mulalic Emir, a policeman who was beaten when questioned. He succumbed to his wounds. And Mr. Sabanovic came, he was escorted by the police, and he said that Emir Mulalic had died of a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How often did you see people being called out and then see them return and -- in cases in which you could tell that they had obviously been beaten? How often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially that was on the 14th of July when the Red Cross arrived in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that? You -- well, first could you answer my question. About how often did you see -- was it just the one time that you saw people called out to be beaten, or how often?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the first week, one week before the arrival -- before the arrival of the Red Cross in Manjaca it occurred every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did things improve after the arrival of the Red Cross? Can you tell me what happened after, you say, the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing improved. It wasn't until later when the Red Cross -- towards the end of August, the food was better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time that you were there, were you personally forced to do any work inside the camp or outside the camp by the guards?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken away to do forced labour. We went to dig canals. People went to build churches. Others went to dig up potatoes. Others went to fell trees and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said the food got better. Was there enough to eat? If you can just give us a general idea of whether you felt you had enough to eat during the day when you were there.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean during the period before the Red Cross started feeding us, or from the time they started providing us with food?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me briefly before and after what the conditions were.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before that, the food was very bad. In the morning we'd get half a cup of tea without any sugar and a slice of bread. And for lunch you'd get a potato and a bit of cabbage, but there was no salt. And then with such food -- having had such food, people would have to go to work. That was when we got up. Because of this lack of vitamins, we had to get up slowly in order to establish our balance, because people often fell over before they were able to stand in a stable manner and to move normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then later on --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, after the Red Cross had arrived, the food was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, just tell us about your release from Manjaca. When did you learn you were going to be released? Or did you learn in advance?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only heard that there were negotiations. But the first group from Manjaca, they were people who -- who had been born in 1953 -- up to 1953, about 700 people left. That was on the 14th of November, 1992. We left after one month, on the 14th of December. And the day before we'd been called out -- but on that morning, when this call-out was to take place, the Red Cross wasn't allowed to enter. They had brought food for us. And policemen came with lists. They entered into each stable and they said, "All the Croats are to take their blankets and go outside. They're to go outside the camp." And then they called out another 300 Muslims from the Prijedor, Sana, and Kljuc areas. So 520 people in total were taken out. They were put into buses, and they left to the -- they went in the direction of the Batkovici camp. And in the afternoon these same people were called out. They were to leave with us. The first group was the 1.040, because there were three phases for leaving, the 14th, and the 18th, and the 20th of December. So these people were called out and they were taken to the Batkovici camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told me about the people who were there with you. If you can just remember, what was the youngest person in your stable and what was the oldest person at any time while you were there, their ages?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some minors, 16 or 17 years old, and up to 62, 63 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you were finally released in December 1992, you eventually reunited with your wife and your child and moved back to Sanski Most some five years later.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of April, 1997, that's when I returned to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned, did you rebuild your house? It's the same one which had been damaged I'm speaking about.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I rebuilt the first floor, what had been damaged, but I didn't find anything in the house. Everything that was there had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who will go first? Yes. Now, Mr. Zecevic, we are proposing to you to have the break now and -- the same break that we intended to have. Instead of having it at ten past or quarter past 5.00, we'll have it now. And then you will have one stretch in which you can conduct and finish -- possibly your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is agreeable. If you prefer to start now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I am fine with the decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Twenty minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Zecevic, who is the lead counsel for General Talic. I must point out to you that Mr. Zecevic has a duty to defend his client, and he will be asking questions not because he has got anything against you but he -- because he has precisely this duty, to defend his client. So please understand that before I give Mr. Zecevic the go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I start, may I ask my learned colleagues from the Prosecutor to provide the witness's statement which was given in September 2001, because I will make a reference. In B/C/S, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Zecevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, my name is Slobodan Zecevic, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. But please, could you make a break after I have put a question to you for the sake of the interpreters, you know.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you gave a statement to investigators for the OTP in September on the 12th and 13th of September, 2001; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Something is wrong with the earphones. I cannot follow the interpreters. That's why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, when you came to The Hague, this statement was certainly shown to you when you spoke to the Prosecution; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In that statement you said, on page 2, the fourth paragraph, that the Serbian defence forces arrived in Sanski Most probably towards the end of 1991 or at the beginning of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you stand by this claim?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that this all took place in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that they arrived, where did they arrive from?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part came. It was the 6th Krajina Brigade, which was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Serbian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbian -- I only know about the 6th Krajina Brigade. And SOS stands for the Serbian defence forces. That's a unit that was established -- was founded in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that unit, the SOS unit, the Serbian defence forces, was founded in Sanski Most. It didn't come from anywhere. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a unit from Sanski Most, and it consisted of men from Sanski Most, from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Njunja was the commander of that unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Saovic, known as Njunja. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page, there are two sentences -- two sentences below the one that you have just read out, you said that the SOS differed from the 6th Krajina Brigade on the basis of their uniforms. At that time they wore camouflage uniforms, and later all soldiers wore camouflage uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 6th Krajina was there when there was an attack. They were wearing reserve uniforms. These were winter uniforms, warm ones, and later on they wore these camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. One moment. May I remind both of you, please, to speak more slowly and to allow an interval between question and answer and between answer and question, because in spite of all the previous exultations, neither of you is following the -- the rule. And I can see -- I can -- I'm following the interpreters. I can see that they are having great difficulties in trying to follow both of you. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, do you know what sort of uniforms the Territorial Defence wore?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they wore olive-drab uniforms. These are winter uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the basis of what these uniforms looked like, you were not able to determine who belonged to a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were reservists who had those warm winter uniforms, and these other men had thinner summer uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "these other people," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the unit led by Dusan Saovic, known as Njunja, the SOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that they wore camouflage uniforms, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on they wore camouflage uniforms. And other witnesses can confirm this. But I didn't see them very often. I only saw them when I was present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us about the fact that sometime in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. February, if I'm not mistaken, a grenade or some sort of explosive device was thrown into the law office of Mr. Sabic's, which is across the road from the court?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was towards the end of February -- and as I worked in the court -- well, yes, that happened in the evening, and we noticed this in the morning when we turned up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, please allow a little bit of time before you start answering -- because you are very quick. Okay? As soon as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As soon as Mr. Zecevic finishes his question, you don't -- you don't give the interpreters a chance to translate it into English or into French to us, so please allow that little bit of time, an interval of time, for the interpreter's sake and for our sake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As this took place -- this happened across the road from the court, you worked in the court, and you are aware of the fact that an investigation was conducted into this; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on that occasion they used dogs too?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I am not aware of that part of the investigation because I was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Sabic, Suad Sabic, the lawyer, he was also a member of the core SDA leadership in Sanski Most; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know, because I don't belong to any party and I had nothing to do with such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that, because I wasn't involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, today when speaking to the Prosecutor, on several occasions you said that during that period, from the end of February up until April, it was mostly business premises, shops belonging to Muslims and Croats -- it was mostly such buildings that were blown up; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And my house too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember that a Serbian cafe was blown up on the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall such an event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you delivered court summons, and you also worked as a driver for the court. You took --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I delivered court summons, but in 1986 I stopped, as a driver, we didn't have a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the investigating judge go to carry out on-site investigations following these explosions?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that. Only two inspectors came to carry out an on-site investigation in my house when my house was blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, given that you delivered court summonses, you probably got around town quite a lot; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I delivered the mail. Naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the SDA in Sanski Most had its own command posts.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The old fire brigade building.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pobrijezje?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I didn't go around the village -- villages. I was only responsible for the town area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- one moment. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question about whether he knew about any of these command posts. He said he didn't know about any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But that was in Sanski Most. Now he was asked about the other place -- whatever it is. I mean -- yeah. So let's -- let's go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Delic, during your examination-in-chief you said -- I think it was on the 15th of April that there was a meeting in court.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Not on the 15th of April. The 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same mistake was made before. And he corrected it, saying that it was the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think now it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was I who said 15th of April, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we're talking of the 15th of May, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, at that meeting you said that you were required to sign an oath of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a kind of oath of loyalty. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was required of the judges. Not of you as well, was it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was required of us too, not just of the judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Delic, when you started working in the court in the former Yugoslavia -- do you need the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's fine. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat. When you started working in the court during the time of the former Yugoslavia, you didn't sign any kind of oath.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That went through the employment bureau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the judges did, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judges were elected and they had to take an oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same applied to prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the positions that required it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you're telling us that on the 15th of May, you too were required to take an oath of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was required of us employees as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not a fact that as a sign of protest or solidarity with the Muslim judges, you stopped going to work?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't want to sign that statement of loyalty, but we would have faired in the same way had we signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement from September 2001 that you gave to the investigators of the OTP, you said that on that occasion there were certain replacements of the president of the court and so on, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the court, the secretary, the deputy prosecutor, and the president of the magistrate courts were replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, the public prosecutor, Slobodan Milasinovic, a Serb, was also replaced, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, again you are not allowing that small interval of time. You're just jumping straight. So please. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, if you know, whether this gentleman, Slobodan Milasinovic also refused to sign this oath of loyalty even though he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you certainly do know that he was replaced as well.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was read out that he was being replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, on the 23rd of May there was an explosive device that was thrown at your house; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that after that you came with your father and brother and that you went to report it to the police while they stayed at home and two policemen came to do the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two inspectors arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, the same statement to the OTP in 2001, on page 3, last paragraph and sentence, they showed you some sort of an official report, that is, the security services centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P206, P206. The Serbian version, please. Yes. I think that's the front -- that's the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other copy, please, put it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, this is a weekly report for the period from the 18th to the 25th of May, 1992, a weekly report issued by the centre of the security services of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of May, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on page 2, the one but last paragraph, under the date the "23rd of May, 1992," it says: "In Sanski Most, at the house owned by Bekir Delic, an explosive device was thrown into the open area."

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my house. It was thrown through the bathroom window, destroying the bathroom and the room I sleep in. All the windows were broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the document that was shown to you in 2001 when talking to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the last page and the signature. The head of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Delic, after that you didn't stay in your house, and on the 26th of May you went to Mahala.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us repeatedly that your house was in a part of town inhabited mostly by Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no real problems, shall I put it that way, with the exception of this explosive device that was thrown at the house.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, but after that I couldn't live there any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecution today, on page 12, lines 22 and 23 of the LiveNote and after that, you said -- not in that statement, in what -- in your testimony today -- you said that you didn't know that anything was in the offing on the 26th of May in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And though you didn't know that anything was about to happen, that morning you went to Mahala, to a house that has a basement. Why?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Passing through Mahala -- as I was passing through the centre of town, there was an APC standing there and next to it was Dusan Saovic standing. They asked me where I was going. I answered I was going to see my father in the Mahala. Then Dusan said, "Let him pass."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you explain to us what APC is, please, or stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to Their Honours what a personal carrier is.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a military vehicle rather like a tank, which has an anti-aircraft machine-gun attached in front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you went to Mahala, you hid in this basement and you said that you heard shooting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at my brother's. We went down to the basement. The shooting started about 9.00. And it was full of women, children, and old people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you heard shooting, rifle shots, and cannon fire?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard the shells, cannon fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that there was a combat going on?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that impression at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, when you came out of the basement, you said in your statement of 2001 that you came across a Serbian paramilitary unit on -- SOS, on page 4, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is right. That was in a part of Mahala, halfway inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was even a problem that occurred. One of them wanted to kill you, and others prevented him from doing that. That is what you said in your statement of 2001.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He separated us males, and he wanted to kill us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this other member of the same unit led you to the Montenegro Cafe, owned by Sarcevic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his cellar where he held the drinks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us today that when you came out on the 27th of May that Mahala was virtually deserted.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were the last to stay there. There was not a soul in Mahala when we came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, this Montenegro Cafe where they put you up in the cellar owned by Sarcevic, that was also in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was already in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next day the owner of the cafe, Mr. Sarcevic, called up the Crisis Staff, and after that the guards withdrew and you left; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked. He didn't know what to do with those people. He said it was very damp and cold and we weren't dressed properly and he didn't know what to do with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to something for a moment. Do you remember what happened on the 19th of April in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when the attack on the municipality took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "attack," is it not true to say that the SDA leaders and the HDZ leaders and policemen had captured the building two days prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the legal elected authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that those policemen who entered the building were armed?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those things. I was not familiar, because I didn't move around in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But they held the building for two days, two whole days. Did you pass by the building of the municipality during that time, from the 19th to the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't move around. This was in the night of the 19th to the 20th, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that you drove Mr. Adil Draganovic to that building?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't escort Mr. Draganovic to that building at all. I didn't accompany him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 18th and the 20th of April, or did you go there with him --

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean his official or private car?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Either.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no contact with Mr. Draganovic, nor did I drive him in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 28th of May. After you left Mahala, you went to another settlement, Narodni front, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a housing estate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that, on the basis of a radio announcement, you reported together with all the other members of your household.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just my mother and father and me, because we had come there from Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, have a break and have some water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- because I'm -- I'm getting worried about this. I mean, the positions -- the respective positions that you've taken, you standing there at the back and Mr. Delic having to literally bend backwards to be able to face you -- not that he needs to face you -- but if you want to take my advice, have a break of two minutes, bring over your papers if it's not too much, and come forward to this empty --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- desk over here --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at least you will be facing together in a manner which is comfortable to both. And I thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just thinking, Your Honour, that it could be helpful if someone who is listening to the English translation could work out some kind of just a little signal to the witness when the translation is finished, at which point he could then begin to answer, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell me how to do it, Mr. Ackerman, and I will -- I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll volunteer just by raising this when he can answer if you want me to do it. I mean, I -- it's -- I'm afraid that the translation is not getting done because it's going too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not on the 4th of July. It will be too much for you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It might be. But someone could probably do that service, and it would help us all. I'm sure. It's up to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think it's really necessary, Your Honour. I mean, I -- why don't we just keep going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I can -- listen, Mr. Nicholls. I can read into --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can read into the stress of the interpreters. I mean, I can read into their voice. They are literally battling to keep up with the rhythm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing that's been done in the past, Your Honour is to have him put his earphones around his neck in English and he can then hear the English. When the English stops --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that could be disturbing to him, that could be disturbing to him. What's being suggested to me by Madam Registrar is to switch on his monitor to the transcript mode, which he will look at, and he will only start giving his answer when he sees that the translation into English has come to a stop. You see that blinking black cursor. And when you see nothing else behind it, that means you can go ahead. You will see that as I talk now, the moment I stop, that blinking black spot, black cursor, stops, and there is nothing behind it. There are words behind it as soon as I start talking again. So we'll try and do it this way. Look at the black cursor. When there is nothing else behind that black cursor, please start giving your answer. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just after you arrived there, your parents were released together with the other older people, women and children, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were then transferred to the gym, and after that to the sports hall; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that sports hall, you met up with your brothers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is when I learnt they were alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent about seven days in that sports hall, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were released because you were living in a part of Sanski Most where the Serbs were in the majority and where there was no war zone.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Tell me please, does that mean that there were no problems in that part of Sanski Most of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because only Serbs lived there as a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "problems," I mean conflicts.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can't be any conflicts if only Serbs were living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other members of the Muslim nation living in that part of Sanski Most were also released home, were they not, together with you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There were a few of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after that you were free to return home, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't feel safe going home. The house was already damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I said that you were free to go, I mean that nobody prevented you from going. If you had wanted to and if you had felt safe in your house, you could have, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Delic. Mr. Zecevic, I don't have the page, line number, et cetera, but earlier on he was asked a question and he said, That was a message. I took it as a message. The moment they threw a bomb or blew up part of my house, it meant don't come here any more. So I think we move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could just say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That wasn't enough, Mr. Nicholls, on my part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Just earlier when the witness was answering a question, counsel went like that a moment ago, because -- and I'd prefer that he not make stopping gestures to the witness while he's answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made this gesture just to slow him down. And after that I said, "Please slow down." That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I tried to be helpful to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Delic, where did you go after this?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to my neighbour's in another district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself chose to go to your neighbour's in another district, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I notice that you have practically lost your voice. If you want to stop and continue tomorrow, we'll stop now and we'll continue tomorrow. What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can continue. I've had a cold for a couple of days, the change of climate I think here. I don't know. It's up to you. I shall try to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it doesn't make a difference. We want to make sure that you don't undergo any undue stress while you are giving evidence. If you are not feeling well -- if you have lost your voice, just tell us and we'll stop, and we'll continue tomorrow. I mean, no one is putting any -- you're not going to finish today in any case. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure, Mr. Nicholls, that he's attended to, because we have a whole sitting tomorrow. May I just ask. How long did you ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I anticipate 45 minutes to 1 hour. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my cross is somewhere between 15 and 30 minutes. It's a little difficult to tell. Somewhere in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we owe it to the witness. I can see that he is suffering. I mean, at first I thought it was just a loss of voice. But if he's telling me that he's got a cold and he's trying to recover from the cold, I mean, it's no use keeping him here and putting him under -- under more undue pressure. The important thing is, Mr. Nicholls, not you directly but through the relative section to make sure that he is given all due attention, to make sure that tomorrow he is -- he is fit to continue his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will talk to the person who does that for our team, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've just got to make some calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering, Your Honour, if you might ask the guards to contact the appropriate people to see if a transport can be arranged so that the accused don't have to sit down in those little holes in the basement until 8.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- Madam Registrar, could you deal with that straight away, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. As well I'm going to inform the victims and witnesses section to take good care of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Sorry about this, Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Ackerman, but I don't think I should continue with the -- we should continue with the -- with the cross-examination in these conditions. I thank you. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15. In the meantime, try to rest, sir, as much as you can. Rest your voice in particular so that tomorrow you will be in a position to continue and finish your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope everything will be fine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. He may be escorted out of the courtroom. In the meantime, General Talic and Mr. Brdjanin, we are going to take -- to do all that is within our power to do -- to ensure that you are not kept here till half past 7.00 or even after. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't promise you miracles, because I was not anticipating to finish at 6.00, but we will do our best. Thank you. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15. I know that the one who is mostly concerned is you, Madam Richterova. But -- I had you in mind, but I think first things come first. Thank you. Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
